reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Characterised by a triad of episodic vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, often with a sense of aural fullness
Vertigo attacks typically last from minutes to hours, distinguishing them from the seconds-long spells of positional vertigo
Hearing loss initially affects lower frequencies and fluctuates, but tends to become permanent and progressive over time
Usually begins unilaterally, though the second ear can become involved in a proportion of patients
The underlying disorder is endolymphatic hydrops, an increase in endolymph volume within the membranous labyrinth
Management principles include dietary salt restriction, diuretics and vestibular sedatives for acute attacks, with lifestyle measures to reduce triggers
Escalating options for intractable disease range from intratympanic therapy to surgical procedures such as endolymphatic sac decompression or labyrinthine ablation
Sudden drop attacks (Tumarkin crises) can cause falls without warning and pose an injury risk
reference.pathophysiology: Meniere's disease is attributed to endolymphatic hydrops, an abnormal accumulation of endolymph that distends the membranous labyrinth. Impaired production, circulation or absorption of endolymph, potentially involving the endolymphatic sac, raises pressure within the scala media. Episodic rupture or dysfunction of the membranes allows mixing of endolymph and perilymph, disturbing the ionic environment of the sensory hair cells and producing acute vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus. Repeated insults cause progressive damage to cochlear and vestibular structures, leading to permanent hearing loss and vestibular hypofunction.
additionalInvestigations: Pure tone audiometry to document fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural loss
Tests of vestibular function such as caloric testing and video head impulse testing
Electrocochleography and other specialised tests where available
MRI of the internal auditory meatus to exclude a vestibular schwannoma
Blood tests to exclude alternative causes when clinically indicated
redFlags: Progressive unilateral hearing loss with tinnitus raising concern for vestibular schwannoma
Neurological signs suggesting a central cause
Sudden severe sensorineural hearing loss requiring urgent assessment
reference.prognosis: The course is variable and unpredictable, with clustered attacks and remissions; vertigo often diminishes over years as vestibular function declines, but hearing loss tends to be progressive and permanent.
pitfalls: Diagnosing Meniere's without excluding a retrocochlear lesion such as acoustic neuroma
Confusing it with vestibular migraine, which can present similarly
Overusing vestibular sedatives beyond acute attacks and impairing compensation
Underestimating the psychosocial and safety impact of unpredictable attacks
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Dietary salt restriction with reduction of caffeine and alcohol as first-line lifestyle measures to limit endolymphatic hydrops
Maintenance diuretic therapy and betahistine to reduce attack frequency
Vestibular sedatives and antiemetics such as prochlorperazine or antihistamines for acute vertiginous attacks
Intratympanic corticosteroid, or ablative intratympanic gentamicin for disabling refractory unilateral disease
Vestibular rehabilitation and hearing aids to manage residual vestibular hypofunction and progressive sensorineural loss
Surgical options such as endolymphatic sac decompression, vestibular neurectomy or labyrinthectomy reserved for intractable vertigo
Audiological monitoring and safety counselling regarding sudden attacks, with ENT specialist follow-up
